items.zh: 如是若內若外六處所攝法，差別分別有六百六十。
items.en: Thus, the dharmas comprised within the six internal and six external sense-fields, distinguished in their differences, number six hundred and sixty.

items.title: Why Each Physical Faculty Is Named What It Is

items.zh: 復次，屢觀眾色，觀而復捨，故名為眼。數數於此聲至能聞，故名為耳。數由此故能嗅諸香，故名為鼻。
items.en: Further, repeatedly observing the many forms, and observing them only to let each one go again — this is why it is called the eye. Again and again hearing wherever sound reaches — this is why it is called the ear. Again and again being able, through this, to smell the many fragrances — this is why it is called the nose.

items.zh: 能除飢羸、數發言論、表彰呼召，故名為舌。諸根所隨，周遍積聚，故名為身。
items.en: Being able to relieve hunger and weakness, repeatedly giving rise to speech, and expressing and calling out to others — this is why it is called the tongue. That which every faculty follows and depends on, and where the elements gather together pervasively — this is why it is called the body.

items.title: Why the Mind Is Named What It Is — Two Kinds of Self-Grasping

items.zh: 愚夫長夜，瑩飾藏護，執為己有，計為我所我及我所。
items.en: Through the long night of ignorance, the ordinary being polishes, adorns, conceals, and protects it, grasping it as one's own, reckoning it as "mine," as "I," and as "the self of the self."

items.zh: 又諸世間，依此假立種種名想。謂之有情、人、與命者、生者、意生、及儒童等。
items.en: Further, based on this, the world at large conceptually posits all manner of names and notions: calling it a sentient being, a person, a life-holder, one who is born, mind-born, or a youth, and so on.
This is why it is called the mind.

items.title: Why Each External Object Is Named What It Is

items.zh: 數可示現，在其方所，質量可增，故名為色。數宣數謝，隨增異論，故名為聲。離質潛形，屢隨風轉，故名為香。
items.en: Repeatedly able to be displayed, occupying its own location, its mass capable of increase — this is why it is called form. Repeatedly proclaimed and repeatedly subsiding, following along to increase various kinds of discourse — this is why it is called sound. Departing from any fixed substance, its shape concealed, repeatedly carried along by the wind — this is why it is called fragrance.

items.zh: 可以舌甞，屢招疾苦，故名為味。數可為身之所證得，故名為觸。遍能任持，唯意境性，故名為法。如是等類，諸法差別應知。
items.en: Able to be tasted by the tongue, repeatedly bringing on sickness and suffering — this is why it is called taste. Repeatedly able to be verified by the body itself — this is why it is called touch. Universally able to sustain its own nature, being solely the domain of mental consciousness — this is why it is called dharma. Differences of dharmas of this and similar kinds should be understood accordingly.
Here a summary verse is given again:

items.title: Five Gateways Through Which Every Kind of Mind Differs

items.zh: 自性及所依、所緣、助伴、業，由此五種門，諸心差別轉。
items.en: Self-nature, and its support; its object, its accompaniments, its activity — by these five gateways, the various kinds of mind turn, each differently.

items.zh: 此中顯由五法、六識身差別轉。謂自性故，所依故，所緣故，助伴故，業故。
items.en: This shows that it is by these five factors that the six classes of consciousness turn, each differently: by self-nature, by support, by object, by accompaniments, and by activity.

items.zh: 又復應知蘊善巧攝、界善巧攝、處善巧攝、緣起善巧攝、處非處善巧攝、根善巧攝。
items.en: Further, it should be understood that this is comprised within six kinds of skill: skill regarding the aggregates, skill regarding the elements, skill regarding the sense-fields, skill regarding dependent origination, skill regarding what is and is not possible, and skill regarding the faculties.

items.title: The Nine Matters That Contain the Buddha's Entire Teaching

items.zh: 又復應知諸佛語言，九事所攝。云何九事？一、有情事，二、受用事，三、生起事，四、安住事，五、染淨事，六、差別事，七、說者事，八、所說事，九、眾會事。
items.en: Further, it should be understood that everything the Buddhas have spoken is comprised within nine matters. What are these nine? First, the matter of sentient beings; second, the matter of enjoyment; third, the matter of arising; fourth, the matter of abiding; fifth, the matter of defilement and purity; sixth, the matter of differentiation; seventh, the matter of the teacher; eighth, the matter of what is taught; ninth, the matter of the assembly.

items.zh: 有情事者，謂五取蘊。受用事者，謂十二處。生起事者，謂十二分事緣起及緣生。安住事者，謂四食。
items.en: The matter of sentient beings is the five aggregates of clinging. The matter of enjoyment is the twelve sense-fields. The matter of arising is the twelve-linked dependent origination, and what arises through it. The matter of abiding is the four foods.

items.zh: 染淨事者，謂四聖諦。差別事者，謂無量界。說者事者，謂佛及彼弟子。所說事者，謂四念住等菩提分法。
items.en: The matter of defilement and purity is the four noble truths. The matter of differentiation is the boundless variety of realms. The matter of the teacher is the Buddha and his disciples. The matter of what is taught is the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, beginning with the foundations of mindfulness.

items.zh: 眾會事者，所謂八眾。一、剎帝利眾，二、婆羅門眾，三、長者眾，四、沙門眾，五、四大天王眾，六、三十三天眾，七、焰摩天眾，八、梵天眾。
items.en: The matter of the assembly is the eight assemblies: first, the assembly of kshatriyas; second, the assembly of brahmins; third, the assembly of householders; fourth, the assembly of renunciants; fifth, the assembly of the Four Heavenly Kings; sixth, the assembly of the Thirty-Three Gods; seventh, the assembly of the Yama-realm gods; eighth, the assembly of the Brahmā gods.

items.title: Closing Verse: All of Fascicle Three in Four Lines

items.zh: 色聚、相應品、世、相、及與緣、善等差別門、巧便、事為後。
items.en: Matter aggregates, the category of what is associated with mind; the times, the marks, and the conditions; the wholesome and its kind, the gateway of differentiation; skilful means, and the matters, come last.

blocks.text: The last reading of fascicle 3, and of the Mind Stage's first long section. The treatise totals its counts, explains why each faculty and object has the name it has, and then gathers everything into larger frames: six kinds of skill, and nine matters that contain all the Buddha's words. It is a short day; use the time to look back over the Mind Stage.

Two short headings are missing from Ru-Yi's translation (now supplied in our own translation, marked as ours): 0294a13, "Here the summary verse is given again", and 0294b02, "A further summary verse".

Each of the twelve sense-fields (six faculties and six objects) has been counted from one to ten ways. One through ten add up to fifty-five; fifty-five times twelve is six hundred and sixty. Venerable Miào Jìng adds a scholar's caution: some lists have no tenth kind (the eye, Day 19: "ten, there is none"), "so six hundred sixty is an approximate figure". Like the eon counts of Day 9, it is a round number standing for completeness.

Each faculty and object is given a meaning for its name. The eye: "repeatedly observing the many forms, and observing them only to let each one go again". Venerable Miào Jìng notes that the second half shows the eye passes from one object to the next; it does not hold. The tongue "removes hunger and weakness, often utters speech, and calls out". Taste "repeatedly brings on sickness and suffering". Master Cháng Bǎi's story for the tongue: it is at once the cheapest and the most precious thing in the world, able to slander and provoke or to praise and reconcile nations, depending entirely on use.

The mind is so named because "ordinary beings, through the long night, polish, adorn, store, and guard it, holding it as their own, reckoning it as 'mine', as 'I', and as 'the self of the self'." Here the treatise touches the root of saṃsāra: grasping at mind as self.
Both teachers, following the *Cheng Weishi Lun*, distinguish two kinds of **self-grasping** (我執):

items: **Innate** (俱生): needs no teaching; constant in the seventh consciousness (which takes the eighth as self) and intermittent in the sixth. It is subtle and removed gradually on the path of cultivation.
**Conceptually constructed** (分別): arises from false teachings and reasoning, only in the sixth consciousness. It is coarse and removed at once on the path of seeing.

blocks.text: This is why, as Day 15 noted, the list of conceits begins with self-conceit as a separate item. The grasping that study can remove is the lesser part; the deeper part needs long cultivation.

Every kind of mind differs through five gateways, and all of this is comprised within **six kinds of skill** (六善巧): skill in the aggregates, the elements, the sense-fields, dependent origination, what is and is not possible, and the faculties. Venerable Miào Jìng: "skill" means wisdom that understands clearly. These six are the standard curriculum of Buddhist analysis, and they recur throughout the treatise.

"All the Buddhas' words" are comprised in **nine matters** (九事): beings, enjoyment, arising, abiding, defilement and purity, variety, the speaker, what is spoken, and the assembly. The matter of defilement and purity "is the four noble truths": suffering and its origin are defilement; cessation and the path are purity.
The fascicle closes with summary verses, an uddāna again (Day 1), compressing all of fascicle 3 into a few lines for memorising.

subs.head: Looking back on the Mind Stage so far

blocks.text: In three fascicles we have seen the mind analysed in every direction: its five aspects; its seventeen powers, from dreaming to dying and rebirth; the formation of the world; and finally a complete classification of everything that can be known. Through all of it run the same few ideas: seeds in the ālayavijñāna, the mental consciousness making karma through attention and volition, and self-grasping keeping the process turning. With fascicle 4 the treatise begins the third to fifth stages, which describe the mind in terms of initial and sustained thought.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, how many are the dharmas of the six internal and six external sense-fields, distinguished in their differences?
options: eighty-seven
one hundred
six hundred sixty
eighty-four thousand
quiz.why: "Thus, the dharmas comprised within the six internal and six external sense-fields, distinguished in their differences, number six hundred and sixty." A is the count for the sphere of dharmas alone; B is the *Hundred Dharmas* treatise. The *Pixunji*'s arithmetic: each of the twelve fields counted one through ten ways sums to fifty-five, and twelve fields make six hundred sixty.

quiz.q: How is "six hundred sixty" arrived at, and according to Venerable Miào Jìng, is it exact?
options: it is exact; every field has exactly one through ten kinds
one through ten sums to fifty-five, times twelve fields is six hundred sixty; but some lack a tenth kind (the eye has "none" for ten), so it is a round figure
it is sixty-six times ten
it is eighty-seven times eight
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "The ten numbers one through ten add up to … fifty-five"; "but as you saw, some have no tenth kind, so the total is not strictly six hundred sixty — six hundred sixty is an approximate figure." The *Pixunji* (cited in Master Cháng Bǎi's lecture) simply counts fifty-five for each of the twelve fields without noting this.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, why is the eye called the eye?
options: because it is most prominent on the face
because it repeatedly observes the many forms, observing each only to let it go again
because it judges good and bad
because it remembers what it has seen
quiz.why: "Repeatedly observing the many forms, and observing them only to let each one go again — this is why it is called the eye." Venerable Miào Jìng cites Kuījī: the Sanskrit *cakṣus* is glossed "going to an end"; "letting go again" shows it passes in an instant and does not continue, and also that it does not discriminate. Master Cháng Bǎi: this matches the eye-consciousness's one-moment sudden mind. C and D are the mental consciousness's work.

quiz.q: The treatise says ordinary beings, through the long night, grasp the mind as "mine," "I," and "the self of the self." Both teachers distinguish innate and conceptually constructed self-grasping. Which is correct?
options: innate self-grasping is inborn, needing no false teaching — constant in the seventh consciousness, intermittent in the sixth, subtle and removed gradually on the path of cultivation; constructed self-grasping arises from false teachings and reasoning, only in the sixth, coarse, and removed all at once at the path of seeing
both are cut at once at the path of seeing
only outsiders have innate self-grasping
constructed self-grasping is in the seventh consciousness
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi, following the *Cheng Weishi Lun*: innate self-grasping is "first, continuous — in the seventh consciousness, taking the eighth's seeing-aspect as self … second, intermittent — in the sixth"; constructed self-grasping "is coarse and so easily removed — at the first path of seeing, contemplating the suchness of selflessness, it is eliminated." Venerable Miào Jìng: innate grasping exists "whether or not one believes in any religion," so C is wrong; constructed grasping is what learning and religion add when people "come up with a whole theory."

quiz.q: The treatise says all the Buddhas' words are comprised in nine matters. What is "the matter of defilement and purity"?
options: the five aggregates of clinging
the four noble truths
the twelve sense-fields
the four foods
quiz.why: "The matter of defilement and purity is the four noble truths." A is the matter of sentient beings, C of enjoyment, D of abiding — all correct content from the same passage. Venerable Miào Jìng: suffering and its origin are defilement, cessation and the path are purity; he praises the treatise for daring to say the Buddha's countless teachings all fall within these nine, "with no tenth."

quiz.q: The treatise says all this is also comprised within six kinds of skill. What are they?
options: skill regarding the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, dependent origination, what is and is not possible, and the faculties
skill in giving, precepts, patience, effort, meditation, and wisdom
skill in hearing, reflecting, cultivating, precepts, concentration, wisdom
skill with the six faculties
quiz.why: "Skill regarding the aggregates, skill regarding the elements, skill regarding the sense-fields, skill regarding dependent origination, skill regarding what is and is not possible, and skill regarding the faculties." Venerable Miào Jìng: "skill" means wisdom — understanding what the aggregates, elements, and the rest are. Master Cháng Bǎi: skill in what is and is not possible is discerning what accords with cause and effect; skill in the faculties concerns the twenty-two faculties; the six are treated at length from fascicle 53 on. B is the six perfections.
